## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Samuddavāṇijajātaka* (Ja 466), translated into English as *The Sea-Merchants*, belongs to the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral]. According to the traditional framing narrative, the Buddha delivered the story while residing at Jetavana concerning Devadatta, after the latter had fallen into hell taking five hundred families with him [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1887]. The opening verse of the text begins with the words *Kasanti vapanti te janā* [Fausböll 1887].

The central narrative relates the story of a village of carpenters who, pressed by debts and unsuccessful in trade, constructed a ship with their own hands and set out across the ocean to emigrate [Eliot 1921; Barua 1921]. Blown by the wind onto an offshore island, they settled there in abundance; the group subsequently divided into two factions, each following its own chief [Barua 1921]. Bhikkhu Sujato identifies the Jātaka as containing a Buddhist version of the classical flood myth [Sujato 2011]. Charles Eliot highlights the story as evidence that maritime voyages and large-scale maritime migrations were familiar themes in ancient Indian society [Eliot 1921]. A verse from this Jātaka also finds a corresponding form in the Prakrit Dhammapada [Barua 1921].

In terms of text reuse and parallels, DharmaNexus detects 14 matching segments between the canonical verses and the fourth volume of the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also records cross-linguistic alignments with the Tibetan translation of the *Jātakamālā* (D4150, with 21 matches) and minor matching segments with the Chinese *Madhyama Āgama* (T 26) [DharmaNexus].
